name: Simte
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Naorem Brojen Singh. 2009. Simte Grammar. PhD thesis, Department of Linguistics, Manipur University, Canchipur (Imphal), 268 pp. Shodhganga hdl:10603/105243. Chapter II 'Phonological System', pp. 9-50.
catalog_locator: Ch. II sec. 2.0 'The phonological system', p. 9; sec. 2.2 Table 3 consonant chart, p. 17; sec. 2.4 'Tone', pp. 49-50.
catalog_quote: [p. 9] In this language, 29 (twenty nine) phonemes are found. They can be divided into segmental and suprasegmental. Number of segmental phonemes are 27 (twenty seven), of which 21 (twenty one) are consonant phonemes and 6 six are vowels. Number of suprasegmentals is two tones, viz. level and falling. [...] [p. 49, 2.4 TONE] Being a Tibeto-Burman language, Simte also has the tonal system. There are two tones in Simte, viz. (a) falling tone /ˋ/ and (b) level tone /ˉ/. Falling tone is marked and level tone is not marked. In this language, tones are limited although some words do have. Some of them are listed below. Examples: LEVEL TONE ɟu 'rat' ... ŋa 'five' ... la 'take' ha 'month' FALLING TONE ɟù 'wine' ... ŋà 'fish' ... là 'song' hà 'teeth'
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

PhD, Shodhganga 10603/105243 = Glottolog ref 319403) and its scanned; rendered pp. 2 and 42 to images and read them directly. Printed p. 9 (p. 2), sec. 2.0: 'In this language, 29 (twenty nine) phonemes are found. They can be divided into segmental and suprasegmental. Number of segmental phonemes are 27 (twenty seven), of which 21 (twenty one) are consonant phonemes and 6 six are vowels. Number of suprasegmentals is two tones, viz. level and falling.' plus Figure 1 'Phoneme hierarchy of Simte' (Suprasegmentals (2) -> Tones (2)) -- verbatim as quoted. Printed p. 49 (p. 42), sec. 2.4 TONE: after a Clark & Yal…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The grammar treats Simte as a (marginally) tonal language with a two-way lexical contrast (level vs falling) on monosyllables; the phonology chapter contains no statement of any kind about word stress or accent placement, so stress position is undescribed in the accessible primary literature.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone the author notes tone is 'limited' (few minimal pairs). Kapginlian 2025 (pp. 116-118), following Ching 2022, instead reports four tones (mid, low, falling-rising, rising-falling) and vowel length, contradicting Naorem's two-tone analysis.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone illustrated on monosyllabic citation forms (nouns/verbs) and a few disyllables; no word- or phrase-level prominence discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Naorem 2009 describes Simte as spoken at Joutung and Simveng-Chiengkonpang (Churachandpur town), Manipur, and states the language 'has no different dialects corresponding to different villages' (ch. I); this is simt1238 proper. Kapginlian 2025 (native speaker, NEHU) covers the same Churachandpur/Thanlon/Singngat community. Note the tonal analyses disagree: Naorem 2009 two tones (level, falling) vs Ching 2022 (via Kapginlian 2025) four tones plus vowel length.
